Kuṟuntokai 130. Veḷḷi Vīti(yār): the confidante / SHE

lg.l: [The confidante] saying, ‘The gossip is great,’ [to the hero]; [the confidante] talking about marriage [offers from] the neighbourhood;
[the confidante] saying, ‘You who talk about the nature of the world, speak [to her yourself]’;
[the confidante] saying, ‘Going through the desert is bearable [for the heroine] with you’;
[the confidante] telling [the hero] the way of coming; [the confidante] persuading [the heroine to take to] the path;
[the heroine’s] speech of lamentation while [still] accepting he is desirable
– [these situations] are suitable, they say, for the encouragement of elopement.

div.p: eṉpatu uṭaṉ pōkku valittal ām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which encouraging elopement occurs.
alar periteṉṟaṉ mutal ākap pāvak kiḷavi yīṟākac collap paṭṭa kiḷavikaḷai yuṭaitteṉṟu colluvar uṭaṉ pōkku valittalai eṉṟa vāṟu.
Beginning with ‘talking about the gossip being great’ and ending with ‘the speech of lamentation’, they say about encouraging elopement that it possesses those aforementioned speech situations.

lg.l: In the seashore village where the white sand is like moonlight,
your consideration for the young woman
with tresses made beautiful with blossoms,Alternatively: ‘beautiful like blossoms’, or ‘that resemble blossoms’. O lord, has become gossip.

div.p: eṉpatu muṉ ṉiṉṟalar periteṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having stood before [the hero] and said, ‘The gossip is great.’

lg.l: The neighbourhood men bring adornments, O lord,

toThis can be construed differently by taking the postposition vayiṉ in the final line with the question in the previous line, and then taking the first line as an independent question: ‘The neighbourhood men bring adornments, O lord. What have [you] decided to do about the girl…’ As I understand the PK sources (see apparatus), their basic structure mimics the translation presented. that veryI take the particle -taṉ in its emphatic sense. I am not quite sure what exactly its function is though. girl with the sapphire-like hair.
What have [you] decided to do [about it]?tuṇivu uṟu ceyti is literally: ‘What action have [you] decided upon?’

div.p: eṉpatu ayal varaivuraittatu.
This is [the confidante] having told [the hero] about marriage [proposals] from the neighbourhood.

lg.l: Like a lotus on a cold winter’s day, my heart slowly turns to misery.
Now, what is fated to be done by those with shining jewels

about the soft-natured girl with a waist slender like lightning?tāmē here is unclear. This is an epicene plural. To what does it refer? Possibly as a pronoun referring to her friends, or perhaps the heroine’s family. If the first, are these girls the agents or the objects of ‘the things to be done’? More likely might be the second, especially in light of the next poem. Viewing this as the first part of a conversation continued in the following poem, then it makes more sense for the heroine’s family to be the referent of tāmē.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻiyait talaimakaṉ viṉāyatu.
This is the hero having questioned the confidante.

lg.l: How would I know, your majesty?

Even if [you] obtained allLit.: ‘in their entirety’, for muḻutum. the four landsPresumably this refers to the four cardinal directions. The idea is to stress that there is nothing in this world that could satisfy the heroine’s family. and the sky,
alas, they would not value [that enough]
for this girl with the ornamented young breast.

div.p: eṉpatu yāṉ aṟiyēṉī yurai yeṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having said [to the hero], ‘I don’t know. You speak [to her]!’

lg.l: If you say [there are] fiery hot things [in the desert],veyya is understood here as a pronominalised neuter singular noun, qualified by the adjective tīya, but it could itself also be an adjective, in which case it could qualify the wilderness.
when she goes with you, O man from the tall distant mountainside,

through the wilderness, they will be whollyThis is meant to mirror the construction from IAC 23 (provided in the apparatus) – peritum iṉiyavām – in meaning, though it necessitates a slightly less common translation of yāvatum than the normal ‘anything’. One can also understand it like that, in which case any- or everything in the wilderness will be pleasant to the heroine. pleasant.

div.p: eṉpatu curañcela vāṟṟuniṉṉōṭeṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having said, ‘Going through the desert is bearable [for the heroine] with you.’

lg.l: Leaving aside the chariot and other things, your duty

is to come to a place near the houseIn the neighbourhood of the house essentially means near or next to it. Such a meaning is attested in AiN 396.2. that no one frequents,payilā literally means ‘unpractised’, so here it refers to a place that no one is ‘practised’ in going to.
O man from the mountainside overflowing with flowers.

div.p: eṉpatu varun tiṟamoḻintatu.
This is [the confidante] having spoken of how to come.

lg.l: As gossip rises up through the village and [our] quarter,
let mother sit alone at home.yāyum tāṉē irukka taṉmaṉaiyāṉē is literally: ‘let mother herself sit in her home’.
After you embraced the warrior with a perfect spear,
he now desires to go through the difficult desert [with you].

div.p: eṉpatu uṭaṉ pōkku nayappittatu.
This is [the confidante] having encouraged [the heroine] to elope.

lg.l: When the rains fall in the forest, it becomes cool,

and the moon in the sky helps without shame.What is the significance of the moon being without shame? Perhaps that the moon is performing its natural role, and when the confidante lies to the foster-mother, she also does so as though she has no shame, thus making it more convincing and natural. Or does the moonlit sky help illuminate their way?
your father’s anger and your mother’s misery
by denyingkāṇa yāṉ maṟuttu literally translates to: ‘by refusing [to say] I saw’. I saw the woman with the sapphire tresses.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: It is pitiable!One could also read this as a rhetorical question – ‘Is it [really so] pitiable?’

This shamenāṇ encompasses ideas of ‘shame’, ‘shyness’, and ‘modesty’. The basic idea here is that by agreeing to elope, she has lost her claim to feel ashamed, i.e., her sense of modesty. has stayed with us for so long.
Now, like the small banks of tall sand with white sugarcane flowers
are worn down and destroyed as the sweet flood takes them,
it does not standkai- functions as a verbal prefix here. There is no clear way to understand it as a noun. as desire crushes it,
having held on as long as it could.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ uṭaṉ cela nērnta pāvak kiḷavi. 20.

This is the heroine’s speech of lamentation, having agreedThis translation is imprecise, but there is no other comfortable way to render the Tamil in English. pāvam is literally the expression of lamentation or regret that one makes, and though this translation renders nērnta as an absolutive, it is actually a relative participle. to elope.
kaḷavu muṟṟum.

standOff.note: Cf. TP225n.3–4: ampalu malaruṅ kaḷavuveḷip paṭukkumeṉ | ṟañca vanta vāṅkiru vakaiyiṉ
Cf. IA22: ampalu malaruṅ kaḷavu ||
Cf. TP115n.8–9: pōkkuṭa ṉaṟintapiṟ ṟōḻiyoṭu keḻīik | kaṟpi ṉākkattu niṟṟaṟ kaṇṇum
Cf. TP198n: tāykku murittāṟ pūkkuṭaṉ kiḷappiṉ ||

There are other mentions of gossip in the TP, but this is the only one that specifically deals with it in this context. Other times, it is mentioned as one of the situations in the married phase of life or with different speakers. Here, what is specifically dealt with is the threat of gossip, which is appropriate to the clandestine phase.

This is another example of C1 transmitting a instead of ai, if one understands this as a simple error, which I do. It seems to be a feature of this MS. For supporting evidence of this conclusion, see the koḷu to the second poem cited in this section of commentary – ayal varaivu uraittatu – which suggests varaivu is the correct reading. However, were one to assume the C1 reading was correct, then varavu could refer elliptically to marriage proposals of the men of the neighbourhood, by stating only that they came.

I do not see why UVC emended here. The only justification I can find is that ulaku iyal kūṟi appears in four NA kiḷavi-s, though never in this context. There is also nothing in the corresponding poem or koḷu that suggests reading kūṟi. Since the C1 reading makes perfectly good sense, and I do not think there is any convincing evidence to emend, I do not follow UVC.

These TP sources are included as they both use the same phrase for this situation – pōkkuṭaṉ – instead of its inversion that became more common – uṭaṉpōkku, which is what is found in the commentary to this verse, for example.
Cf. AV166.2: alaraṟi vuṟuttal
Cf. AV166.3: piṟarvarai vuṇarttal
Cf. IAC23, p. 157: tōḻi eṉṉai viṉavaṟpālai yallai, nī itaṟkut takkavāṟaṟintu ceyaṟpālaiyeṉṉum
Cf. AV182.2: avaḷuṭaṉ paṭuttal

The wording of the AV parallel is terse and elliptical, but it is made clear from the example in the commentary that the traditional interpretation of this phrase aligns with what one finds in the TNV.
Cf. IAC23, p. 158: emperumāṭṭi! namperumāṉ nammait tammōṭu uṭaṉkoṇṭu cellak karutukiṉṟār, niṉkuṟippeṉṉai eṉṉum.
Cf. AV182.3–4: pāṅki | talaivik kuṭaṉpōk kuṇarttal
The IAC quotes no poem to exemplify this situation, but just presents this snippet of an exchange between the heroine and confidante, where the confidante informs her of the hero’s desire to elope.
Cf. AV182.4–5: talaivi | nāṇaḻi piraṅkal
Cf. NA227.9 (IAC23, p. 155): kauvaiyā kiṉṟa taiyaniṉ ṉaruḷē ||
Cf. PK169.4 (IAC23, p. 155): alarāy viḷaikiṉṟa tālaṇṇa ṉīceyta vāraruḷē ||
Cf. PK170.3–4 (IAC23, p. 155): aṇṇal vantuceyta | varuṭā ṉalarāy viḷaikiṉṟa tāṉmaṟṟiv vāyiḻaikkē ||
Cf. TK180.4: alarāy viḷaikiṉṟa tampalkaim mikkaiya meyyaruḷē ||

Cf. PK171 (IAC23, p. 156): nīraṇi vēli neṭuṅkaḷat toṉṉār niṇamāḷainta | pōraṇi vēṉmaṉṉaṉ kaṉṉiyaṉ ṉāṭaṉṉaip poṉṉaṇivāṉ | kāraṇi vārmura cārppap piṟaruṅ karutivantār | vāraṇi pūṅkaḻa laṇṇale ṉāki valittiṉṟatē ||

Cf. PK173 (IAC23, p. 156): pōrmali tevvaraip pūlantai veṉṟāṉ pukāraṉaiya | vārmali koṅkai maṭantaiyai vēṟōr maṇaṅkarutik | kārmali vārmura vārppap piṟaruṅ karutivantā | rērmali tāraṇṇa leṉṉō vitaṉṟiṟat teṇṇuvatē ||
Cf. TK195: maṇiyak kaṇiyu maraṉañca mañci maṟukiviṇṇōr | paṇiyak karuṇai tarumparaṉ ṟillaiyaṉ ṉāṭiṟantut | tuṇiyak karutuva tiṉṟē tuṇituṟai vāniṟaipoṉ | aṇiyak karutukiṉ ṟōpalā mēṉmē layalavarē||
Cf. IAC23, p. 157: iṇṇaṉañ collappaṭṭa talaimakaṉ eṉṉāṟ ceyyappaṭṭatu eṉṉōveṉṉum.

In C1, the first eḻuttu is not totally clear. It seems to be a hastily written na, which bears some resemblance to a ta, though it does not look tremendously similar to examples of either from the surrounding text. Can one read nāmē? ‘We’ would then be the agent of what is to be done. This would require an awkward syntactic construction. ilaṅku iḻai would be a qualifier left without a head-word that, by the rules of standard Tamil syntax, should immediately follow it. One would then either have to understand it as another qualifier of the heroine, or as a bahuvrīhi-type compound, referring to the heroine. Neither of these makes sense considering the locative postposition tiṟattu attached to the bahuvrīhi-type compound functioning as an ākupeyar (‘metonymy’, essentially) for the heroine in line two.

The IAC passage cited is not the most exact source, but Nakkīrar does not quote a poem for exactly this situation. He simply reports the rhetorical question the hero asks and I believe this question is the source for the poem quoted in the TNV.

Cf. PK177 (IAC23, p. 157): eṉṉā lituceykeṉ ṟeṉcolla lāmikaṟ pāḻiveṉṟa | miṉṉā rayiṟpaṭaic ceṅkōl vicāritaṉ vīṅkolinīrt | teṉṉā ṭeṉiṉuṅkoḷ ḷārvilai yāttamar cīrceyvaṇṭu | muṉṉāṇ malareṉ ṟaṇaiyuṅkaṇ ṇēḻai mukiḻmulaikkē ||

Cf. TK266: kuṟaiviṟkuṅ kalvikkuṅ celviṟku niṉkulat tiṟkumvantōr | niṟaiviṟku mētaku nītikku mēṟpiṉal lāṉiṉaiyiṉ | iṟaiviṟ kulāvarai yēntivaṇ ṭillaiya ṉēḻpoḻilum | uṟaiviṟ kulānuta lāḷvilai yōmeymmai yōtunarkkē ||
Cf. KT388.7: kāṉamu miṉiyavā nummoṭu variṉē ||
Cf. PK178.3–4 (IAC23, p. 158): vemmaiyaṅ kāṉa meṉiṉumav vēntaṉceyya | kōlpurai taṉmaiya vānummo ṭēkiṉak kompiṉukkē ||
Cf. PK179.3–4 (IAC23, p. 158): aḻalaṇi vemmaiya vāyiṉuṅ kāṉa mavaṉkuṭaiyi | ṉiḻalaṇi taṉmaiya vānummo ṭēkiṉen nēriḻaikkē ||
Cf. IAC23, p. 157: aṉṉa veṅkāṉa meṉiṉum emperumāṭṭi nummoṭuvarap peritum iṉiyavāmeṉṉum.

Cf. TK202: piṇaiyuṅ kalaiyumvaṉ pēyttē riṉaipperu nīrnacaiyāl | aṇaiyu murampu nirampiya vattamu maiyameyyē | iṇaiyu maḷavil lāviṟai yōṉuṟai tillaittaṇpūm | paṇaiyun taṭamumaṉ ṟēniṉṉō ṭēkiṉam paintoṭikkē ||

The KKms reading, adopted by Cām, possibly makes better sense, but C1 is also perfectly sensible. There are no strong parallels I have found for the comparative tīyiṉum, so I am not convinced by the KKms evidence alone. Here, I feel comfortable going with the lectio difficilior, which is C1. The KKms reading would also be a tempting emendation on account of the metre, as it would retain the prosodic structure of the first cīr in all three lines. Since this is not a consistent feature of the TNV poems, I did not consider this as strong evidence.
Cf. AN220.1: ūruñ cēriyu muṭaṉiyain talareḻa
Cf. AN383.2: ūruñ cēriyu mōrāṅ kalareḻa

Presumably this was a scribal error in C1 – uḷa (உள) and ū (ஊ) look similar. The AN sources cited above (AN 220 and 383) strongly suggest that C2 etc., read the correct text. One can make sense of uḷarum, though, as an imperfective peyareccam, in which case one could translate the first line as: ‘As gossip rises up through all the agitated quarter’.
Cf. TK214.1–2: īṇtollai yāyamu meḷavaiyu nīṅkavivvūrk kavvaitīr | tāṇṭollai kaṇṭiṭak kūṭuka nummai
Cf. PK180.3–4 (IAC23, p. 159): cēṇu makalā tuṭaṉeṉṉo ṭāṭit tirintuvanta | nāṇu maḻiyat takukaṟpu mēmpaṭa naikiṉṟatē ||
Cf. TK208: maṟpāy viṭaiyōṉ makiḻpuli yūreṉ ṉoṭumvaḷarnta | poṟpār tirunāṇ poruppar viruppup pukuntununtak | kaṟpār kaṭuṅkāl kalikkip paṟitteṟi yakkaḻika | iṟpāṟ piṟavaṟka vēḻaiyar vāḻi yeḻumaiyumē ||
The IAC quotes KT 149 to exemplify this situation as well.
